questions.q: How does short-selling make money, according to the summary?
a: By borrowing shares, selling them, then buying them back cheaper
By holding shares for decades and collecting dividends
By buying shares just before an earnings report
By lending money to struggling companies
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes borrowing a stock at its current price, selling it, and rebuying it after the drop.

questions.q: What is the snowball effect in the summary?
a: Riding a rally as other investors pile in
Selling everything before a market crash
Spreading money across many industries
Borrowing to buy more of a losing stock
questions.why: Lesson 1 says hedge funds buy early in a rally because crowd psychology accelerates the rise.

questions.q: What did the fund Farallon do differently from its rivals?
a: It held traders accountable for losses as well as gains
It hired traders with no experience at all
It avoided short-term trading entirely
It paid bonuses only for long-term holdings
questions.why: Lesson 2 says accountability for losses encouraged moderate, careful investing.

questions.q: What bet did George Soros win big on in the 1980s?
a: The fall of the dollar
The rise of gold prices
The collapse of the housing market
The success of Japanese stocks
questions.why: Lesson 2 says he bet against the dollar when few believed it could collapse.

questions.q: Why does the summary say banks are a bigger threat than hedge funds?
a: Their finances are interconnected, creating a domino effect
They take far riskier bets on new companies
They are entirely unregulated by governments
They hold most of the world's hedge fund money
questions.why: Lesson 3 says banks and governments are financially linked, so one failure can pull down the other.
